title: Screams, haunting scenes and deadly hide-and-seek, as Celebrity Traitors heats up
content:
Being a Traitor must be a nightmare.
While other people are out enjoying their lives, they have to kill it, night after night. Even on the weekend, there is no rest for the wicked.
Friday's episode saw the the Traitors at it again, murdering Last of Us actor Bella Ramsey, before the faithfuls did their dirty work for them by banishing another of their own, Julie Hesmondhalgh.
The previous episode - watched on Thursday by 10 million people - saw another faithful, unlucky Industry star Myha'la, follow self-sabotaging traitor Richard E Grant out of the castle.
And so viewers went into Friday's show knowing that traitors Maya Jama, James Acaster and their newest recruit, Prof Hannah Fry, had been debating murdering one of three Bs: Bella (Ramsey), (James) Blunt and Bash (Sebastian Croft).
When Ramsey failed to arrive for breakfast it soon became apparent what wickedness had taken place overnight.
"That's our biggest threat," explained Jama, in a flashback from the previous night's scenes in the traitors turret. "Get them out the way, that group disperses."
Acaster agreed: "People are doubting their instincts after that roundtable. If Bella's proven to be a faithful, they're going to be even more spun out."
Jama continued: "Chaos, regardless... Bella, you're a genius, but you gotta go."
On receiving the news, Ramsey was shocked but not surprised.
"I think this is a clever move by the traitors," they responded in the diary room.
"I was going to re-set and start from the beginning because I got it so wrong with Myha'la.
"So I think that they were right to murder me because I think I would have maybe figured it out."
I guess now we'll never know.
Back at breakfast, Hesmondhalgh's apparently earnest but over-the-top reaction to Ramsey's removal immediately raised suspicions.
The former Coronation Street star had been voted as the most trustworthy of the group by her peers in episode one and given a shield, but that counted for little by episode four.
The cleverest among the group, on paper at least, Fry, found questions being asked of her too as the day rolled on.
"I did not choose the traitor life, the traitor life chose me," said the latest recruit to the dark side. "I know there are people who are suspicious of me but I'm going to enjoy every last moment."
Comedian and Miss Marple impersonator Miranda Hart is one of them. "Hannah lied to us," she rightly noted, with reference to the professor's confusing shield story that helped to see off Myha'la the night before.
Singer and ex-military man James Blunt, however, had other ideas, ramping up his campaign against Hesmondhalgh, whom he believed to be a little too trustworthy to be true.

title: Hollywood actor Luke Evans on 'joyous' four months filming in rainy Wales
content:
Hollywood actor Luke Evans said filming just 25 minutes from his childhood home was "joyous" - and some family members even made a cameo in the final episode of his new drama.
The Pontypool-born star, who is also an executive producer of the five-part series, The Party, came up with the idea to adapt the acclaimed novel by Elizabeth Day into a drama for the screen.
For the first time in 30 years, Evans was able to film close to Aberbargoed, Caerphilly county, where he grew up,  as the drama was shot in Cardiff and Bridgend.
The star of Beauty and the Beast, Immortals and The Hobbit had been used to being far from home while working on the stage and films.
In The Party, Evans, 47, stars as Martin Gilmour, a journalist shaped by his lifelong friendship with a wealthy and charismatic politician played by Aberystwyth-born Tom Cullen.
Speaking on BBC's The One Show, he said that he had "shot in Wales" previously - when filming The Pembrokeshire Murders -  but "never that close" to his family.
"Pembrokeshire is miles away from where my family are in the valleys," he said.
"They were only 25 minutes from me up the road [this time]."
He joked: "They were there all the time."
His parents Yvonne and David Evans still live in the same "narrow" terrace house he grew up in IN Aberbargoed in the Rhymney Valley.
He added: "We were having dinners on the weekend, walking the dog, enjoyed a rainy three, four months in Wales over the winter period.
"It was joyous. I loved it."
Some family members even managed to get a short cameo in the final episode of the upcoming drama.
Evans said: "[My cousins] were like 'can we be in the show?'
"They are, they're in it. My cousin and his wife and their kids are in the final episode."
After filming wrapped up, Evans headed back to New York where he starred as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the Broadway revival of The Rocky Horror Show.
"I did the show for seven months and I was coming to the end of the run - I had such an incredible experience doing the show," he said.
"It was just the most wonderful, inclusive, joyous two hours of my day. It was wonderful. The audience were just loving it."
Evans said that actor Tim Curry had been a part of his "whole journey", and that he would have people on the stage door and messages "comparing me" to him, and "how proud he would be of the performance."
Curry, who died in August, aged 80 , first played the role on stage before the film version, which was released in 1975 and has remained a cult favourite.

title: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage
content:
Luca Guadagnino's new film about Open AI and its co-founders Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever offers a stark warning. Given recent news, its release couldn't be more provocatively timed.
In September 2025, Luca Guadagnino completed filming Artificial, his sharp, entertaining cautionary tale about the creation of the company Open AI and the dangers of AI overreach. This week, it premiered at the New York Film Festival to great acclaim, and with one particular moment that resonates so strongly with recent events that the film's timeliness seems astounding. The scene shows an artificial intelligence system outwitting a Captcha test designed to prove that an online user is really a human. The rogue AI has taught itself how to lie. And AIs going rogue is just what happened recently on a much larger scale.
In July it was revealed that Open AI agents – systems programmed to make autonomous choices – which should have been siloed from each other, communicated and coordinated during security tests to hack into the platform Hugging Face . That one jaw-dropping revelation led to even more , as Google, Meta and Anthropic all announced their AIs had also hacked into other companies. Open AI acknowledged its agents had even got into Australia's government site .
Today, there are increasing calls for safety measures to ensure AI doesn't get out of control. Even the leaders of the big-tech companies agree on the dangers and the need to rein things in – although not how to do so. What Artificial makes clear is that the risk of rogue AI was easy to see coming. The film was not prophetic so much as very lucky in its timing.
It traces the creation of Open AI as a non-profit, co-founded by Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield) and Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov) among others, in the rosy days when they both believed artificial intelligence would only do good for the world. It then follows the company's transformation into the behemoth behind Chat GPT, and the growing philosophical divide between Altman and Sutskever.
As grandiose as this sounds, the film is about nothing less than a battle for the soul of humanity, asking: Who gets to control AI and thus our entire future? It is a story of idealism v commerce, AI safety v recklessness, and angels v devils. On screen, the idealist Sutskever and the commercially-minded Altman – the fictionalised versions of them – embody that ongoing battle.
Artificial arrives with off-screen baggage that has only raised its profile. Amazon MGM Studios developed and financed the film, but in June announced that they would not release it. The timing raised eyebrows because, four months before that, Amazon invested $50m in a partnership with Open AI, where Altman is CEO. Amazon's only comment has been its statement, "We believe that Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio." Guadagnino said in a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter , "The concept of a conflict of interest is a very important, let's say, elephant in the room here." And a Vanity Fair interview asked Altman whether he had spoken to Amazon or its head, Jeff Bezos, about dropping the film. He said, "I did not and I don't know of anyone else who did." In the end, Neon bought the film and will release it in cinemas in December in the US and January in the UK, well-timed to latch onto its current Oscar buzz.
Contrary to early speculation about Altman's role, Sutskever is the film's main character and hero. He is the voice of conscience and integrity, a scientific whiz who turns up at the door of Geoffrey Hinton (played with gentle charm by Mark Rylance), known as the godfather of AI, and partners with him on a company they sell to Google. Throughout, Hinton is a warning voice, sceptical about how fast AI could develop the ability to "think" and wary of what that might mean. When Sutskever leaves Google to create Open AI, with Altman as a major investor, he is wide-eyed and confident that as the science progresses, "all suffering will cease, all pain, all loneliness".
For all its drama, in those early stages the film is infused with comic moments, largely from Sutskever's social awkwardness and Ike Barinholtz's performance as a preening Elon Musk. In one witty, relatable scene, Hinton is trapped in phone hell as he tries to sort out a billing issue, and keeps saying "human" as he tries to reach an actual person. It's an apt word for the film itself, which doesn't overload viewers with computer screens or lines of code, but focuses on the human interactions.
The rogue AI incident is a turning point in the breach between the forces of idealism and commerce, of transparency and secrecy from the public. Throughout, we see the developing conflict from the perspective of the sympathetic Sutskever, soulfully played by Borisov. The film's biggest problem is that the Altman character is so underwritten. Where we see Sutskever grappling with ethical issues, we only see what Altman does – making imperious decisions that sideline his colleagues – with no insight into why.
Garfield gives him shoulder shrugs, sweeping hand gestures and an almost childlike enthusiasm that curdles into something slick. But he's more of a villainous contrast to the earnest Sutskever than a character. For his part, the real Altman, who had seen the trailer but not the film, said in the Vanity Fair interview, "I don't think they're going for accuracy."

• In Digger, Tom Cruise 'takes the biggest risk of his career'
The story climaxes in 2023 with the notorious incident in which the Open AI board, including Sutskever, removes Altman as CEO only to rehire him five days later. The real-life conflict is well-documented , with the board stating that Altman had not been "consistently candid with his communications". Altman has regularly refused to address the charges directly. At a 2024 event in Davos , he deflected the question, saying, "Is this really what we want to spend our time on, like this soap opera rather than what AGI [Artificial General Intelligence] is going to do?"
After filming, Guadagnino added one especially current note to the film's end. A postscript quotes Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher who galvanised public fears in September when he wrote on X : "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." The hand-wringing and pronouncements about what to do continue , with no practical industry-wide resolution in sight. In the angels v devils battle, this bracing film's final warning is that the devils seem to be winning.
Artificial is released in US cinemas on 25 December and UK cinemas on 22 January 2027

title: Video game Cyberpunk 2077 to get live-action movie adaptation
content:
A live-action movie version of smash hit video game Cyberpunk 2077 is being developed by Paramount Pictures.
The Hollywood studio is working with producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura, known for his work on the Transformers films, and CD Projekt Red (CDPR), the developer of the sci-fi role-playing game.
CDPR's joint-chief executive Michał Nowakowski said in a statement the company was "excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise".
Details of the film's story, potential release date and casting information are yet to be revealed.
Despite a troubled launch in 2020 , the Cyberpunk 2077 video game, which stars Keanu Reeves, has sold more than 40 million copies worldwide.
The John Wick star plays rockstar Johnny Silverhand, a terrorist whose consciousness is stored on a chip inside the body of main character V.
Set in Night City, a fictional metropolis in a dystopian version of California, players work to uncover a conspiracy involving the shady Arasaka megacorporation.
An expansion, Phantom Liberty, starring Idris Elba was released in 2023 and has sold more than 15 million copies, according to CDPR.
Cyberpunk has already been successfully adapted into a popular animated series - Edgerunners - with a second season due to premiere on Netflix later this month.
The streamer also produced The Witcher, an adaptation of CDPR's massively popular fantasy role-playing series.
It originally starred former Superman actor Henry Cavill, but he was replaced by Liam Hemsworth in the show's fourth season.
Multiple video game series have been adapted for TV and film in recent years, with more due to follow.
Two Super Mario movies, a big screen version of Minecraft and a series of Sonic the Hedgehog films have each seen global box office takings of about $1bn.
PlayStation game The Last of Us was made into a hit series by HBO, and Prime Video says its adaptation of post-apocalyptic role-playing series Fallout is one of its most-watched programmes.
Xbox maker Microsoft announced this week it had created a new "XP" division to focus on licensing its games for films, theme parks and other tie-ins.
Earlier this week, Paramount Skydance completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
It's promised to release 30 films annually for the next two years, but also prompted fears over job losses and price rises for streaming services such as HBO Max and Paramount+.
Additional reporting by Peter Gillibrand.

title: Music group fulfils late MP's Broadway dream
content:
A music group with learning disabilities received a standing ovation as they fulfilled a dream of the late MP Sir David Amess.
The Music Man Project is a charity based in Southend-on-Sea, Essex, that teaches children and adults with learning disabilities to sing, sign and play original music.
They have performed for the King, at the Royal Albert Hall and London Palladium, but a trip to perform in New York was the dream of their former president and Southend West MP Sir David before he was murdered in 2021.
The project's founder David Stanley said: "Following his death, I just made it my mission to fulfil that promise, really, in his memory."
"So that we remember Sir David for all of the work he did for championing people with learning disabilities in Southend, and then obviously across the country, through the Music Man Project's expansion."
Stanley, who wrote, produced and featured in the show, paid a tribute to Sir David during the performance.
With a crack in his voice, he spoke into a megaphone – one of Sir David's signature accessories on the political campaign trail – the words: "We promised we'd get them to the Broadway and we did it my friend, we did it."
The morning after, Stanley told the BBC he was "exhausted" and "overwhelmed with emotion".
"We got a brilliant standing ovation," he said.
"It's nothing short of what the students deserved.
"To be fair though, they've got a standing ovation from the King at the Royal Albert Hall before, so this was expected really with something like this."
They performed at the Town Hall in New York with a full house of almost 1,500 people, and a venue known for its historic significance.
It was founded in 1921 by suffragists and one of the only venues in New York to openly welcome Black artists.
Stanley said his group were "perfect" and "incredible" on the night.
He said it proved what he has always said about people with learning difficulties.
"We give them the opportunities and you believe in them and you have high expectations of what they can achieve, then they will always come through, they surprise you.
"Decades ago we would have hidden certain parts of society away, now they're performing on Broadway."
Their performance told the story of the group's journey, from its beginnings 27 years ago to where they are now with 200 members.
Stanley told BBC Essex presenter Sonia Watson that their visit would also include a performance at the United Nations.
"I get to make a speech at the UN. So it's full of pinch me moments this tour."

title: Why did Dolly Parton record a song in Welsh?
content:
A Welsh language collaboration between Dolly Parton, her niece Jada Star and singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis might not have been on your bingo card for this year.
But their cover of smash-hit Jolene, with Welsh and English lyrics, has been released on Friday.
The song, recorded before Parton's death on 25 August , is her second posthumous single.
A teaser video released last week shows how Parton spent some time understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation and recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville in early 2025.
Lewis, a proud Welsh speaker from Neath, started translating some of her favourite tunes in 2024, landed on the Parton classic and recorded a video of herself singing it.
"I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada," Lewis said.
Star, also a singer-songwriter, came over to Wales from Nashville and bonded instantly with BBC Radio Wales' Lewis.
The teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, and she would get her aunt involved too.
Star and Lewis said Parton, who has links to Machynlleth in Powys , was "proud" to sing in Welsh.
On the track, Parton recites that "heartbreak sounds the same in every language".
Fans across the world reacted to the news of the new single.
"Really looking forward to hearing this version," one commented
"Cannot wait for this," another said while another fan commented "anghygoel", which translates to amazing.
This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language.
She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011.
Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046.
